title: The banyan seed
hook: break a seed, see nothing, and learn what holds up the whole tree
carry: the unseen essence holds up the world

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tree, struck at root, middle and top, bleeding but alive. Your line was the body dies; the self does not.
screen: `THE TREE — THE BODY DIES. THE SELF DOES NOT.`

segments.voice: A banyan doesn't stop at one trunk. It sends roots down from its branches, and those roots thicken into new trunks, until one tree can look like a small forest. Birds nest in it, people sit in its shade, and all of it is one tree. Its fruit is a little fig a bird could swallow whole, with seeds like specks of dust inside. Uddalaka sends his son to fetch one.
screen: `A TREE THAT LOOKS LIKE A FOREST.` → `ROOTS THAT BECOME TRUNKS.` → `IT STARTED AS A TINY SEED.`

segments.voice: The lesson is a short conversation, almost a game. Bring me a fruit from that banyan. Here it is, sir. Break it. It's broken, sir. What do you see? These tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them. It's broken, sir. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir. And the father says: my dear, that subtle essence you can't see, from that very essence this great banyan tree stands. Believe me, my dear. He doesn't describe the seed. He has his son break it with his own hands and look, and the son reports honestly: nothing. That nothing is the point. Not empty nothing. Too-fine-to-see nothing. Uddalaka's word is anima, the subtlest. Here is the Hindu teaching: what's most real isn't the biggest thing in the room. It's the unseen essence that everything you can see stands on. Then he asks for shraddha, faith: shraddhatsva, believe me. Not belief instead of looking; his son has just looked as hard as anyone can. In this story, faith comes after looking, at the edge of what eyes can do. So when a classmate asks, where's God, under a microscope? Uddalaka's son already tried that with a seed. Look as closely as you like. The tree is still standing. Then the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this world. You are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` · `WHAT DO YOU SEE? NOTHING AT ALL.` · `ANIMA: THE SUBTLEST.` · `SHRADDHA: FAITH, AFTER LOOKING.` · then, large: `FROM THAT, THIS GREAT TREE.`

segments.voice: Start with something big in your life, your body, your family, your work, and go smaller, the way the son broke the fruit and then the seed: what's this made of, and that? When you reach the edge of what you can see, don't force an answer; rest there.
Anima, the subtlest, the finest. Broken open, the banyan seed shows nothing at all; from that unseen, subtle essence, the father says, the great banyan stands.
Your line: the unseen essence holds up the world. From that, this great tree stands. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The banyan is sacred to many Hindus and is often worshipped, especially by women during the Vat Savitri festival; teachers use Uddalaka's banyan seed to explain the subtle essence behind the visible world.
